notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on 1 John 1, drawn from the sources listed below. I have indicated where I found each point and noted where I could not obtain material from certain traditions or sites.

---

## Overview of the Chapter

John opens without a personal greeting, leaping straight into a declaration of what (or rather, *whom*) he and the other apostles have personally experienced. The chapter falls into two parts: (1) the prologue on the incarnate Word of Life (vv. 1–4), and (2) the message that “God is light” with its practical tests of fellowship and sin (vv. 5–10). Most teachers agree the letter combats an early form of Gnosticism (or proto-Gnostic tendencies) that denied either the real humanity of Jesus or the reality of sin in believers.

---

## v. 1 – “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands—this is the Word of life.”

- **The “beginning.”** There are two main conservative interpretations. Some (John Piper, John Stott, Robert Lightner, Utley) understand it as eternity past, echoing Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1 — thus affirming Christ’s pre-existence and deity. Others (A. W. Pink, F. F. Bruce, John MacArthur, D. Edmond Hiebert) take it as the beginning of the gospel era — i.e., the start of Jesus’ earthly ministry, stressing that the apostolic message is unchanged from the earliest days. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1john_11_commentary)

- **The four sense-verbs (heard, seen, gazed upon, handled).** John piles up hearing, seeing, intense looking (“gazed upon”), and touching to counter early Gnostic teachers who claimed Jesus was a phantom (Docetism). The perfect tense of “heard” and “seen” in Greek indicates abiding results: what John heard and saw decades earlier still rang in his ears and stayed in his mind’s eye. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1john_11_commentary); [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **“Word of life.”** Gill explains that this title belongs to Christ because He has life in Himself as God, as Mediator, and as man, and is the author of natural, spiritual, and eternal life. The phrase “Word” (Logos) is the same as in John 1:1, and was meaningful to both Jews (God revealed through His Word) and Greeks (the Logos as the ultimate Reason governing the universe). John is saying: “This Logos you have discussed for centuries — we have heard, seen, and touched Him.” [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm); [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **The neuter “That which”** (Greek: *ho*). The neuter pronoun probably encompasses both the message about Jesus and the person of Jesus Himself. The gospel is a message, a person, and a lifestyle. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1john_11_commentary)

---

## v. 2 – “And this is the life that was revealed; we have seen it and testified to it, and we proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us.”

- **“The life was manifested.”** The eternal life that was “with the Father” (implying distinct personhood within the Godhead) was made physically real and visible in history. John is an eyewitness, not a spinner of myths. Gill notes that Christ was “manifested in human nature” in a way the patriarchs and prophets never experienced — they saw Him in promise and type, but the apostles saw Him incarnate. [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm); [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **“Eternal life.”** Calling Jesus “eternal life” itself (not merely the giver of eternal life) underscores His deity. People may be “eternal” in the future sense (immortal), but only God is eternal in the past sense — without beginning. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **“With the Father.”** The Greek preposition *pros* (“with”) indicates both distinction from the Father and face-to-face relationship. This builds the NT understanding of the Trinity. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

---

## v. 3 – “We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us. And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ.”

- **“Fellowship” (Greek: *koinōnia*).** This is a key word in 1 John. It means a sharing of common life and resources, not just a friendly acquaintance. G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik) calls it “one of the greatest statements of the New Testament.” Acts 2:44 uses the same word: believers “had all things in common” (*koina*). The staggering claim is that believers share a common life with God the Father and His Son. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/); [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1john_11_commentary)

- **“So that you also may have fellowship with us.”** John first mentions fellowship with the apostolic circle, then with God. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) notes: “When fellowship is the sweetest, your desire is the strongest that others may have fellowship with you.” Often people first encounter God through relationships with God’s people. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Gill** adds that believers’ fellowship with the Father includes, under the Spirit of adoption, calling God “Father,” drawing near through Christ, and enjoying the discoveries of His love. Fellowship with the Son means being admitted to intimacy, brought into His banqueting house. [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm)

---

## v. 4 – “We write these things so that our joy may be complete.”

- **“Our joy” or “your joy.”** Manuscripts differ: some read “our joy,” others “your joy.” Either way, John’s aim is fullness of joy — a joy rooted in fellowship with God, not in circumstances. John echoes Jesus’ words in John 15:11, 16:24, and 17:13 about joy being made full. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/); [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm)

- **Spurgeon (cited by Guzik):** “If any of you have lost the joy of the Lord, I pray you do not think it a small loss.” Fullness of joy is possible for the Christian but not automatic; it must be actively pursued through fellowship with God. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **The Pulpit Commentary** (Homiletics) notes that the readers’ joy had been incomplete because their knowledge of Christian truth had been partial. Fuller disclosure brings fuller joy — the joy of forgiveness, of reconciliation, of progress in holiness, and of hope of glory. [Pulpit Commentary on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_john/1.htm)

---

## v. 5 – “And this is the message we have heard from Him and announce to you: God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.”

- **“God is light.”** This is a summary of the message John received from Jesus Himself. Light signifies God’s absolute purity, holiness, truth, and perfection. Adam Clarke (cited by Guzik): “LIGHT is the purest, the most subtle, the most useful, and the most diffusive of all God’s creatures; it is, therefore, a very proper emblem of the purity, perfection, and goodness of the Divine nature.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Maclaren (cited by Guzik):** “There are spots in the sun, great tracts of blackness on its radiant disc; but in God is unmingled, perfect purity.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Gill** notes that “no darkness at all” means no darkness of sin, no darkness of error or ignorance, and no variableness or shadow of turning — God is always the same pure, holy, wise, and knowing Being. [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm)

- **John Piper** calls this the “theological foundation” for the whole paragraph (vv. 5–10): because God is light, any problem in our fellowship with Him is on our side, never His. [Desiring God sermon summary](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-us-walk-in-the-light-of-god) (content inferred from search excerpt; full page unavailable due to fetch limit)

- **John MacArthur** stresses that John begins this section with “God is light” to lay the groundwork for the first test of genuine salvation — one’s attitude toward sin. A true believer acknowledges sin; a false one hides or denies it. [GTY sermon](https://www.gty.org/sermons/62-4/the-certainty-of-sin-part-1)

---

## v. 6 – “If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.”

- **“Walk in darkness.”** This means a *pattern* or lifestyle of sin — not an occasional lapse. John speaks of a habitual walk, not a momentary stumble. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Gill:** To “walk in darkness” is to be in a state of unregeneracy — understanding darkened, ignorant of Christ and His righteousness, preferring darkness and loving the works of darkness. If such a person claims fellowship with the God who is light, they lie; it is a contradiction. [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm)

- **A key interpretive divide:** Some (like Guzik / Enduring Word) see this as about *fellowship*, not salvation — a true Christian can temporarily walk in darkness and lose fellowship with God (but not salvation). Others (like MacArthur / Piper) see this as a *test of regeneration*: a lifestyle of walking in darkness proves one’s claim to know God is false. For MacArthur, “walking in darkness” describes the unregenerate, not a backslidden believer. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/); [GTY](https://www.gty.org/sermons/62-4/the-certainty-of-sin-part-1)

---

## v. 7 – “But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin.”

- **“Walk in the light.”** Guzik interprets this as a generally obedient life, without harbouring known sin or resisting the Holy Spirit’s conviction. It does *not* mean sinless perfection; otherwise there would be no sin to cleanse in the ongoing sense. Walking implies activity, continuity, and progress. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **“The blood of Jesus … cleanses us.”** The Greek verb is present tense: it speaks of *continual* cleansing. As we walk in the light, Jesus’ blood keeps on purifying us from every sin. This is not a once-for-all cleansing at conversion only, but an ongoing reality. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **“Fellowship with one another.”** Strikingly, John does not say “fellowship with God” here (that is already implied by walking where God is). Instead he says that walking in the light produces fellowship *among believers*. If two Christians lack fellowship with each other, at least one of them is not walking in the light. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Gill:** Walking in the light means being enlightened by the Spirit, having a true sight of sin, knowing Christ and the way of salvation, being a child of the light, and walking as Christ walked. Such walkers enjoy fellowship with one another and the ongoing cleansing of Christ’s blood. [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm)

- **Piper:** From the search excerpt, Piper notes two things accompany walking in the light: (1) fellowship with one another, and (2) the cleansing of Christ’s blood. The walk is a lifestyle resulting from new birth. [Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-us-walk-in-the-light-of-god)

---

## v. 8 – “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

- **“We have no sin.”** This targets those who claim they have no sin *nature* or *principle* of sin within them — i.e., those who claim to have reached a state of sinless perfection. John says such a claim is self-deception. [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm); [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Contrast with v. 10.** Verse 8 uses the noun “sin” (*hamartia*) — claiming to have no sin principle. Verse 10 uses the verb “have not sinned” — claiming never to have committed sinful acts. John refutes both. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Piper:** The claim of sinlessness is simply self-deception. Instead of denying our sinfulness, we should confess that it is real and ugly. The wonderful promise of verse 7 (“cleanses us from all sin”) could be abused by perfectionists; John immediately clarifies: you are not without sin — you need continual cleansing. [Desiring God (search excerpt)](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-us-walk-in-the-light-of-god)

- **MacArthur:** Regenerated people confess their sin as a pattern of life. Unregenerated people tend to conceal or deny the seriousness of their sin. The first test of genuineness is one’s perspective on sin. [GTY](https://www.gty.org/sermons/62-4/the-certainty-of-sin-part-1)

---

## v. 9 – “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”

- **“Confess” (Greek: *homologeō*).** Literally, “to say the same thing” — to agree with God about our sin. Guzik stresses this means personal, specific, honest confession, not vague admissions like “we all make mistakes.” [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **“Faithful and just.”** God’s forgiveness is grounded in His own character. He is faithful to His promises and just (righteous) because Jesus has already paid the penalty for sin. The righteousness of God is not our enemy but our friend — it *guarantees* forgiveness because Christ’s work satisfied divine justice. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Gill:** This promise is for believers. When they sin, they are to be humbled, confess it before God, and He will forgive and cleanse. It is not to be expected that believers be entirely clear of sin in this life, only that they confess it as often as they sin. [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm)

- **MacArthur** strongly emphasises that confession of sin is absolutely basic to salvation. Against those who teach that one can be saved without confessing sin, MacArthur points to the Bible’s “amazing record of confessions” — from Pharaoh, Saul, David, Daniel, Peter, the prodigal son, the tax collector, and Paul. Confession is not optional; it is a certain proof of salvation. [GTY](https://www.gty.org/sermons/62-4/the-certainty-of-sin-part-1)

---

## v. 10 – “If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us.”

- **“We have not sinned”** (perfect tense). This targets those who deny they have ever committed acts of sin. Such a claim goes beyond self-deception (v. 8) into blasphemy — it makes God a liar, because God has declared in His word that all have sinned (e.g., Romans 3:23). [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Piper:** “The sentence, ‘I am without sin,’ amounts to the sentence, ‘God is a liar.’” The claim to sinlessness is not only self-deception but blasphemy. [Desiring God (search excerpt)](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-us-walk-in-the-light-of-god)

- **“His word is not in us.”** Gill explains this means the truth of grace is not in such a person, nor is the word of God dwelling in them. They have no true knowledge of God’s word and no place for it. [Gill on biblehub](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm)

- **MacArthur** sees this verse as the strongest warning in the passage: the person who denies ever having sinned proves that God’s word has no place in them — they are unregenerate. [GTY](https://www.gty.org/sermons/62-4/the-certainty-of-sin-part-1)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The main points of difference found in the sources consulted:

### 1. Fellowship vs. Salvation (vv. 6–7)

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** “Walking in darkness” describes a believer who is out of fellowship. The issue is *fellowship*, not salvation. A Christian who temporarily walks in darkness is still saved but not enjoying communion with God. Confession restores fellowship. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)

- **Reformed Baptist (John MacArthur, John Piper):** “Walking in darkness” is characteristic of the *unregenerate*. The tests in 1 John serve to distinguish true believers from false. A lifestyle of walking in darkness proves one’s claim to know God is false. Confession is a mark of genuine salvation, not merely a means of restoring fellowship. [GTY](https://www.gty.org/sermons/62-4/the-certainty-of-sin-part-1); [Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-us-walk-in-the-light-of-god)

### 2. The Meaning of “From the Beginning” (v. 1)

- **Eternity past view** (John Piper, Utley, Henry Morris): Emphasises Christ’s pre-existence and deity, linking 1 John 1:1 to Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1john_11_commentary)

- **Gospel-ministry view** (MacArthur, F. F. Bruce, A. W. Pink, Hiebert): Emphasises the unchanged apostolic message from the start of Jesus’ earthly ministry, countering Gnostic claims of new, secret knowledge. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1john_11_commentary)

### 3. “We have no sin” (v. 8) — Sin Nature or Sin Acts?

- Some Wesleyan/Holiness traditions teach that entire sanctification can eradicate the sin nature in this life. John’s statement “if we say we have no sin” is sometimes understood in those traditions as referring to *acts* of sin, not the sin nature, or as a warning against a wrong kind of perfectionism. I was unable to access Wesleyan sources (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) within search limits, so I cannot report their specific reading.

- The Reformed and Baptist sources consulted all read “sin” in v. 8 as the sin principle or nature, and see v. 10 as addressing sinful acts. Both are denied by the false teachers John opposes.

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship / NET Bible notes:** The NET Bible note (cited on Precept Austin) observes that the Greek prologue of 1 John 1:1-4 is a single, awkward sentence, and that a literal translation produces “almost impossible English.” This grammatical observation does not change the interpretation but highlights John’s breathless, urgent style. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1john_11_commentary)

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I was unable to access newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search and fetch limits. From general knowledge of Catholic exegesis (not directly confirmed from the allowed sites in this session), Catholic teaching on 1 John 1:9 has traditionally supported the sacrament of Penance (confession to a priest), but I cannot cite a specific page from the permitted sources to support this. I must leave this section incomplete.

**Hyper-grace / modern popular teaching:** Some modern teachers (not directly cited in the pages fetched) have argued that 1 John 1:9 is written to unbelievers or to Gnostics, not to Christians, and that believers therefore need not confess sins for forgiveness — they are already forgiven. I found no page among those fetched or searched that represents this view, so I cannot describe it from the sources. The sources I did read (Guzik, MacArthur, Piper, Gill) all treat 1 John 1:9 as addressed to believers and as describing ongoing Christian practice.

---

## Summary of Sources Used

- **Enduring Word (David Guzik)** — Pentecostal/Charismatic: [1 John 1 Commentary](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-john-1/)
- **Precept Austin** — Evangelical, compiling many writers: [1 John 1:1 Commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1john_11_commentary)
- **Gill’s Exposition** (BibleHub) — Older Baptist: [1 John 1 Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_john/1.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary / Homiletics** (BibleHub): [1 John 1 Pulpit Homiletics](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_john/1.htm)
- **John MacArthur / Grace to You** — Reformed Baptist: [The Certainty of Sin, Part 1](https://www.gty.org/sermons/62-4/the-certainty-of-sin-part-1)
- **John Piper / Desiring God** — Reformed Baptist (search excerpts; full fetch unavailable): [Let Us Walk in the Light of God](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let-us-walk-in-the-light-of-god)

**Not obtained due to search/fetch limits:** Wesleyan/Methodist (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes beyond the excerpt on Precept Austin), and hyper-grace sources.
